what_its_for: Trifluoperazine is used to treat schizophrenia and other mental health conditions that cause symptoms like hallucinations (hearing or seeing things that are not there), confused thinking, and unusual behavior. It may also be used for short-term relief of severe anxiety. It belongs to a group of medicines called antipsychotics, which help balance certain chemicals in the brain.
how_to_take: Take this medicine by mouth exactly as your doctor tells you. You can take it with or without food, but taking it with food or a full glass of water may help reduce stomach upset. Try to take it at the same time each day to help you remember. Do not crush or chew tablets unless your doctor or pharmacist says it is okay. Do not stop taking this medicine suddenly without talking to your doctor first, as stopping abruptly can cause problems.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your condition and how you respond to treatment. Doses vary widely from person to person. A common starting dose for adults with schizophrenia is 2 to 5 mg taken twice daily. Your doctor may slowly increase your dose over time. For anxiety, doses are typically lower. Always follow your doctor's instructions and never change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist for advice.
storage: Store trifluoperazine at room temperature, between 59°F and 77°F (15°C and 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep this medicine out of reach of children and pets. Do not use it after the expiration date printed on the label. Ask your pharmacist how to safely dispose of any unused medicine.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking this medicine, as it can increase dizziness, drowsiness, and other side effects. Do not drive, operate heavy machinery, or do anything that requires you to be alert until you know how this medicine affects you. Avoid getting overheated or dehydrated, especially in hot weather or during exercise, as this medicine can make it harder for your body to cool down. Avoid getting up too quickly from a sitting or lying position, as this medicine can cause your blood pressure to drop suddenly and make you dizzy. Avoid prolonged sun exposure and use sunscreen, as this medicine can make your skin more sensitive to sunlight.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the nearest emergency room if you experience: uncontrolled muscle movements of the face, tongue, lips, or body (this could be a serious condition called tardive dyskinesia); muscle stiffness, high fever, sweating, fast or irregular heartbeat, or confusion (signs of a rare but serious condition called neuroleptic malignant syndrome); difficulty breathing or swallowing; severe dizziness or fainting; unusual mood changes or thoughts of harming yourself; yellowing of the skin or eyes; or signs of infection such as fever, sore throat, or mouth sores. Also contact your doctor if you feel more restless than usual or have trouble sitting still.
when_it_works: You may start to notice some improvement in your symptoms within the first few days to weeks of starting this medicine. However, it may take several weeks of regular use to feel the full benefit. It is important to keep taking your medicine even if you do not feel better right away. Do not stop taking it without talking to your doctor first.
special_populations: Older adults: This medicine should be used with extra caution in elderly patients, especially those with dementia, as it may increase the risk of serious side effects including stroke and death. Older adults are also more sensitive to dizziness and falls. Pregnancy: Talk to your doctor if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. This medicine may cause movement problems or withdrawal symptoms in newborns if taken during the last trimester of pregnancy. Breastfeeding: This medicine may pass into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding. Children: Dosing in children is based on weight and age, and should only be used under close medical supervision. Liver or kidney problems: Tell your doctor if you have any liver or kidney problems, as your dose may need to be adjusted.
